## Infant of a Diabetic Mother

questions.stem: Central cyanosis in a newborn is best assessed by examining which sites?
questions.initialExplanation: Central cyanosis is visible in the tongue and mucous membranes and generally reflects low arterial oxygen saturation due to respiratory or cardiac disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. The tongue and oral mucosa are the key sites for central cyanosis.
- B. Scalp and back are not the defining sites.

- C. Nail beds alone are less reliable for distinguishing central from peripheral cyanosis.
- D. Blue hands and feet alone may represent peripheral cyanosis.
- E. Abdominal skin alone does not establish central cyanosis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Examine the tongue and mucosa to distinguish central cyanosis from peripheral acrocyanosis.

questions.stem: A cyanosed newborn receives 100% oxygen during a hyperoxia test, but the arterial PaO2 remains low. Which cause is favored by standard guidance?
questions.initialExplanation: Failure of PaO2 to rise substantially during a hyperoxia test favors a right-to-left cardiac shunt from cyanotic congenital heart disease; respiratory causes generally show improvement.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. RDS is a pulmonary cause and is expected to respond to oxygen and respiratory support to some extent.
- B. TTN is a pulmonary cause and may show oxygenation improvement.
- C. Persistent low oxygen despite 100% oxygen supports cyanotic CHD in the hyperoxia-test framework.
- D. Peripheral acrocyanosis does not cause persistently low arterial PaO2.
- E. Neonatal acne has no effect on oxygenation.
questions.highYieldPoints: - A poor response to 100% oxygen suggests a right-to-left cardiac shunt; use echocardiography for definitive assessment.

questions.stem: Which medication may be started urgently in a cyanosed newborn when a duct-dependent congenital heart lesion is suspected?
questions.initialExplanation: Recommended management includes prostaglandin E infusion when duct-dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease is suspected, while urgent cardiac assessment and echocardiography are arranged.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Phenobarbital is an anticonvulsant.
- B. Prostaglandin E maintains ductal patency in duct-dependent lesions.
- C. Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
- D. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
- E. Caffeine citrate is used for apnea of prematurity.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Suspected duct-dependent CHD is an emergency; prostaglandin maintains ductal patency pending cardiology assessment.

questions.stem: Which definition of neonatal apnea is used?

options.label: A
options.text: Cessation of breathing for at least 20 seconds, or a shorter pause associated with bradycardia or cyanosis

options.label: B
options.text: Cessation of breathing for at least 5 seconds in each case

options.label: C
options.text: Any irregular breathing pattern during sleep

options.label: E
options.text: cessation of breathing associated with fever

questions.correctAnswerText: Cessation of breathing for at least 20 seconds, or a shorter pause associated with bradycardia or cyanosis
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal apnea is defined as cessation of breathing for at least 20 seconds, or any shorter duration if associated with bradycardia or cyanosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the definition stated.
- B. Five seconds alone is insufficient unless associated with clinical signs.
- C. Periodic breathing may be irregular without meeting the definition of apnea.
- D. A respiratory rate below 60/min is not apnea.
- E. Fever is not required.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Duration plus associated bradycardia or cyanosis defines clinically significant apnea.

questions.stem: Why does an infant of a diabetic mother commonly develop hypoglycemia shortly after birth?

options.label: A
options.text: Fetal hyperinsulinemia persists after the maternal glucose supply is interrupted at birth

options.label: B
options.text: The newborn has excessive glucagon secretion

options.label: C
options.text: The placenta continues to deliver glucose after birth

options.label: D
options.text: Maternal insulin crosses the placenta and suppresses fetal glucose

options.label: E
options.text: The newborn cannot absorb glucose from the intestine

questions.correctAnswerText: Fetal hyperinsulinemia persists after the maternal glucose supply is interrupted at birth
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal insulin production. After delivery, the maternal glucose supply stops but fetal hyperinsulinemia persists, causing hypoglycemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the pathophysiology described.
- B. Excessive glucagon would tend to increase glucose rather than cause this mechanism.
- C. Placental glucose delivery stops at birth.
- D. Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta in clinically significant amounts.
- E. Intestinal glucose absorption is not the mechanism.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Maternal hyperglycemia → fetal hyperinsulinemia → interruption of glucose supply after delivery → neonatal hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: Which blood glucose value meets the hypoglycemia threshold stated for an infant of a diabetic mother?
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe neonatal hypoglycemia in this context as blood glucose below 2.6 mmol/L or approximately 45 mg/dL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is not hypoglycemia.
- B. This is elevated rather than low glucose.
- C. The threshold is not below 10 mmol/L; that would classify many normal values incorrectly.

- D. This is the threshold stated.
- E. This is hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Standard guidance's threshold is <2.6 mmol/L (approximately 45 mg/dL); follow local neonatal thresholds in practice.

## Birth Injuries

questions.stem: Which symptom may indicate hypoglycemia in a newborn of a diabetic mother?
questions.initialExplanation: Neonatal hypoglycemia may be asymptomatic or present with jitteriness, poor feeding, apnea, convulsions, lethargy, or pallor.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Sneezing alone is not a typical manifestation.
- B. A port-wine stain is a vascular skin malformation.
- C. An umbilical hernia is not a sign of hypoglycemia.

- D. A positive Ortolani test indicates hip instability or dislocation.
- E. These are recognized symptoms of neonatal hypoglycemia.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Hypoglycemia may be subtle; check glucose in at-risk infants even if symptoms are nonspecific.

questions.stem: Which electrolyte abnormality may present with jitteriness or seizures in an infant of a diabetic mother, often around the second day of life?
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include transient hypoparathyroidism and hypocalcemia in infants of diabetic mothers, typically presenting around the second day with jitteriness or seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hypernatremia is not the specific association listed.
- B. Hypercalcemia is the opposite abnormality.
- C. Hypermagnesemia is not the typical complication described.
- D. Hyperphosphatemia is not the defining neonatal IDM complication.

- E. Hypocalcemia is the electrolyte issue described.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Consider hypocalcemia when jitteriness or seizures occur after the first day in an IDM.

questions.stem: Which cardiac condition is associated with infants of diabetic mothers?

options.label: A
options.text: Coarctation of the aorta as the association

options.label: C
options.text: Tetralogy of Fallot as the defining lesion in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with interventricular septal hypertrophy

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with interventricular septal hypertrophy
questions.initialExplanation: Infants of diabetic mothers may develop hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, often involving interventricular septal hypertrophy; many are asymptomatic and the finding may resolve over weeks to months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Coarctation is not the only or main association described.
- B. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is not a neonatal IDM complication.

- C. TOF is not the defining association stated.
- D. Atrial myxoma is unrelated.
- E. This is the cardiac complication described.
questions.highYieldPoints: - IDM-associated septal hypertrophy is often transient but can cause respiratory or heart-failure symptoms.

questions.stem: Which congenital anomaly is described as particularly specific for maternal diabetes?
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include sacral agenesis as a particularly specific congenital anomaly associated with maternal diabetes, while cardiac defects are the most common overall.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Cleft palate can occur in many contexts and is not the specific association highlighted.
- B. Choanal atresia is associated with CHARGE.
- C. Sacral agenesis is specifically highlighted as a characteristic association.
- D. Neural tube defects are associated with maternal diabetes but are not the specific anomaly asked.

- E. Congenital cataract is associated with congenital infections such as rubella.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Cardiac anomalies are common overall; sacral agenesis is the particularly specific association mentioned.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes caput succedaneum from cephalohematoma?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are caused by intracranial bleeding

options.label: B
options.text: Cephalohematoma is diffuse and crosses most sutures

options.label: C
options.text: Caput succedaneum is subperiosteal and cannot cross sutures

options.label: D
options.text: Caput succedaneum is a diffuse subcutaneous fluid collection that crosses suture lines

options.label: E
options.text: Cephalohematoma is present immediately in typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: Caput succedaneum is a diffuse subcutaneous fluid collection that crosses suture lines
questions.initialExplanation: Caput succedaneum is a diffuse subcutaneous fluid collection present immediately after birth that can cross suture lines; cephalohematoma is a subperiosteal blood collection limited by sutures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Neither condition is defined as intracranial bleeding; both are extracranial scalp collections.

- B. Cephalohematoma is localized and does not cross sutures.
- C. This describes cephalohematoma, not caput.
- D. This is the distinguishing feature of caput succedaneum.
- E. Cephalohematoma may become apparent hours after birth rather than immediately.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Caput crosses sutures; cephalohematoma is confined by sutures.

questions.stem: A newborn develops a large, diffuse, boggy scalp swelling after vacuum-assisted delivery. The swelling extends widely and the infant becomes pale and hypotensive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.initialExplanation: Subgaleal hemorrhage is bleeding into the subaponeurotic space. It can spread widely and cause severe blood loss, hypovolemic shock, and coagulopathy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This diffuse boggy swelling with shock is characteristic of subgaleal hemorrhage.
- B. Salmon patch is a benign pink vascular macule.

- C. Caput is a superficial fluid collection and is not usually associated with severe blood loss.
- D. Cephalohematoma is localized under periosteum and limited by sutures.
- E. Milia are small white papules.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Subgaleal hemorrhage is a potentially life-threatening cause of neonatal blood loss after instrumental delivery.

questions.stem: A newborn has an adducted, internally rotated shoulder, extended elbow, and pronated forearm after shoulder dystocia. Which nerve roots are most likely injured?
questions.initialExplanation: Erb-Duchenne palsy is an upper brachial plexus injury involving C5–C6, producing the classic waiter's-tip posture.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. C8–T1 injury causes Klumpke palsy, often with claw hand.
- B. Lumbosacral roots supply the lower limb.

- C. Thoracic roots do not form the brachial plexus roots described.
- D. C3–C4 injury may affect the phrenic nerve but is not the classic upper trunk injury.
- E. C5–C6 injury causes Erb palsy and the waiter's-tip posture.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Erb palsy = upper plexus C5–C6; Klumpke palsy = lower plexus C8–T1.

questions.stem: Which reflex pattern is characteristic of Erb-Duchenne palsy?

options.label: A
options.text: Absent Moro reflex with preserved grasp reflex

options.label: B
options.text: Absent grasp reflex with preserved Moro reflex

options.label: C
options.text: Normal Moro with absent rooting reflex

options.label: E
options.text: Both Moro and grasp reflexes absent in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Absent Moro reflex with preserved grasp reflex
questions.initialExplanation: In Erb palsy, the Moro reflex is reduced or absent on the affected side, while the grasp reflex is preserved because the lower plexus roots are intact.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the reflex pattern described for upper plexus C5–C6 injury.
- B. This pattern is more consistent with lower plexus involvement such as Klumpke palsy.
- C. Rooting reflex is not the specific discriminating reflex pattern.
- D. Sucking reflex is not the described distinguishing feature.

- E. Both reflexes are not necessarily absent; the pattern depends on the roots involved.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Erb palsy: absent Moro, preserved grasp.

questions.stem: A newborn has a claw hand following a difficult delivery. The grasp reflex is absent, while the Moro reflex is preserved. Which injury is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Klumpke palsy is a lower brachial plexus injury involving C8–T1 and may cause claw hand, absent grasp reflex, and sometimes Horner syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Phrenic nerve palsy affects diaphragmatic function.
- B. Erb palsy affects C5–C6 and produces waiter's-tip posture with absent Moro.
- C. Klumpke palsy affects C8–T1 and produces claw hand with absent grasp.
- D. Clavicle fracture may cause pseudoparalysis and an asymmetric Moro reflex, but not the characteristic claw hand.

- E. Facial nerve palsy affects facial expression muscles.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Claw hand with absent grasp suggests C8–T1 lower plexus injury.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve injury may cause unilateral facial weakness after instrumental delivery?

options.label: A
options.text: Upper motor neuron trigeminal nerve lesion

options.label: B
options.text: Lower motor neuron facial nerve (VII) palsy

questions.correctAnswerText: Lower motor neuron facial nerve (VII) palsy
questions.initialExplanation: Facial nerve palsy after instrumental delivery is usually a peripheral (lower motor neuron) lesion, producing weakness of the whole ipsilateral face.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. The trigeminal nerve is not the motor supply for facial expression.
- B. This is the type of injury described.
- C. The hypoglossal nerve controls tongue movement.
- D. The oculomotor nerve controls most extraocular muscles and eyelid elevation.

- E. The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
questions.highYieldPoints: - A peripheral facial nerve injury affects the entire ipsilateral half of the face.

questions.stem: What is the commonest fracture in the newborn, often associated with shoulder dystocia?
questions.initialExplanation: Clavicle fracture is described as the commonest neonatal fracture and may follow shoulder dystocia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Skull base fracture is rare and serious.
- B. Clavicle fracture is the commonest neonatal fracture listed.
- C. Vertebral fracture is not the commonest birth fracture.

- D. Humeral fractures can occur but are less common than clavicle fracture.
- E. Femoral fractures are less common and may occur with difficult delivery.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Consider clavicle fracture after shoulder dystocia, especially with an asymmetric Moro reflex or crepitus.

## Neonatal Jaundice

questions.stem: At approximately what serum bilirubin level does jaundice usually become clinically visible in a newborn?
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that neonatal jaundice becomes clinically apparent when serum bilirubin rises above approximately 5 mg/dL.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fifteen mg/dL is a much higher bilirubin level.

- B. Three mg/dL is generally below the clinical visibility threshold stated.
- C. Five mg/dL is the approximate threshold given for visible jaundice.
- D. Two mg/dL is near the normal reference value.
- E. One mg/dL is usually not visibly apparent as jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Visible neonatal jaundice is usually apparent when bilirubin exceeds about 5 mg/dL.

questions.stem: Which statement about unconjugated bilirubin is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is lipid-soluble and circulates bound to albumin

options.label: B
options.text: It cannot cross the blood–brain barrier under any circumstances

options.label: C
options.text: It is excreted unchanged into bile without hepatic processing

options.label: D
options.text: It is produced by intestinal bacteria

options.label: E
options.text: It is water-soluble and freely excreted in urine

questions.correctAnswerText: It is lipid-soluble and circulates bound to albumin
questions.initialExplanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and travels in plasma bound to albumin. When albumin binding is exceeded, free unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood–brain barrier.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This correctly describes unconjugated bilirubin transport.
- B. Free unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood–brain barrier and cause neurotoxicity.

- C. Unconjugated bilirubin must be conjugated in the liver before biliary excretion.
- D. Bilirubin is produced mainly from heme breakdown, not only by intestinal bacteria.
- E. This describes conjugated bilirubin, which is water-soluble.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Albumin binding limits free unconjugated bilirubin; free bilirubin is the neurotoxic fraction.

questions.stem: Conjugation of bilirubin in the liver is mainly performed by which enzyme?
questions.initialExplanation: Hepatic glucuronyl transferase conjugates unconjugated bilirubin, making it water-soluble so it can be excreted in bile.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Amylase digests starch.
- B. Lactase digests lactose at the intestinal brush border.
- C. Acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine.

- D. Glucuronyl transferase catalyzes bilirubin conjugation.
- E. Alkaline phosphatase is a marker of cholestasis and bone activity, not the conjugating enzyme.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Immature glucuronyl transferase activity contributes to physiological neonatal unconjugated jaundice.

questions.stem: Which feature is more characteristic of conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia?

options.label: A
options.text: typically physiological in the first week

options.label: C
options.text: Dark urine and pale stools in obstructive jaundice

options.label: E
options.text: Normal urine color and dark stools

questions.correctAnswerText: Dark urine and pale stools in obstructive jaundice
questions.initialExplanation: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is water-soluble and may cause dark urine and pale stools when bile flow is obstructed; it does not cause kernicterus in the way unconjugated bilirubin does.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Direct hyperbilirubinemia is pathological and requires evaluation.
- B. Hepatomegaly and liver dysfunction may accompany conjugated jaundice.

- C. Dark urine and pale stools are characteristic of cholestasis or biliary obstruction.
- D. Kernicterus is associated with free unconjugated bilirubin.
- E. This describes the usual pattern of unconjugated jaundice more closely.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Direct jaundice suggests hepatobiliary disease; dark urine and pale stool are important clues.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cause of increased unconjugated bilirubin production in a newborn?

options.label: C
options.text: Hemolysis due to Rh or ABO incompatibility

questions.correctAnswerText: Hemolysis due to Rh or ABO incompatibility
questions.initialExplanation: Hemolysis from Rh or ABO incompatibility increases bilirubin production; other causes include G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis, bruising, cephalohematoma, and polycythemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Choledochal cyst causes biliary obstruction and direct hyperbilirubinemia.
- B. Alagille syndrome is a cholestatic disorder.
- C. Hemolysis increases heme breakdown and unconjugated bilirubin production.
- D. Biliary atresia causes conjugated cholestasis.
- E. PFIC causes cholestasis and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Hemolysis and extravasated blood increase unconjugated bilirubin production.

questions.stem: A newborn develops jaundice during the first 12 hours after birth. How should this be regarded?

options.label: C
options.text: typically pathological until an underlying cause is excluded

questions.correctAnswerText: typically pathological until an underlying cause is excluded
questions.initialExplanation: Jaundice during the first 24 hours is always considered pathological and requires evaluation for hemolysis, infection, or other causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Early jaundice may be unconjugated or conjugated and is not defined by bilirubin fraction alone.

- B. Normal transitional jaundice does not usually appear in the first 24 hours.
- C. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological and requires prompt investigation.
- D. Breast milk jaundice typically appears later, often from the second week.
- E. Physiological jaundice typically begins after the first day.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Jaundice in the first 24 hours is a red flag and should never be assumed physiological.

questions.stem: Which pattern is most consistent with physiological neonatal jaundice in a healthy term infant?

options.label: B
options.text: Jaundice with sepsis and temperature instability

options.label: C
options.text: Direct bilirubin elevation with pale stools

options.label: D
options.text: Onset in the first 12 hours with rapid rise

options.label: E
options.text: Onset after the first day, predominantly indirect bilirubin, and a well infant

questions.correctAnswerText: Onset after the first day, predominantly indirect bilirubin, and a well infant
questions.initialExplanation: Physiological jaundice typically begins on day 2, is unconjugated, occurs in a well infant, and peaks around day 4 in term infants.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Anemia and organomegaly suggest hemolysis or systemic disease.
- B. Sepsis and temperature instability are pathological features.

- C. Direct jaundice and pale stools suggest cholestasis.
- D. First-day jaundice is pathological.
- E. This is the typical physiological pattern described.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Physiological jaundice begins after 24 hours in a clinically well newborn and is predominantly unconjugated.

questions.stem: Which rate of bilirubin rise is considered a feature of pathological neonatal jaundice?
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include a bilirubin rise greater than 5 mg/dL per day as a feature of pathological jaundice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A rate below 1 mg/dL/day is not the pathological threshold given.
- B. A rise in bilirubin is expected in the neonatal period; the rate and clinical context matter.

- C. This is below the threshold.
- D. This is below the threshold stated.
- E. A rise above 5 mg/dL/day is the pathological rate listed.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Rapid rise, early onset, illness, or a direct fraction are warning features.

questions.stem: 's updated definition, prolonged neonatal jaundice is jaundice lasting more than:

options.label: A
options.text: 7 days in term and 14 days in preterm infants

options.label: C
options.text: 4 weeks in term and 6 weeks in preterm infants

options.label: E
options.text: 2 weeks in term infants and 3 weeks in preterm infants

questions.correctAnswerText: 2 weeks in term infants and 3 weeks in preterm infants
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance uses a threshold of more than 2 weeks in term infants and more than 3 weeks in preterm infants for prolonged jaundice.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This reflects an older definition mentioned, not the updated threshold used.
- B. Three months is longer than the threshold used.

- C. Four and six weeks are later than the threshold given.
- D. Six weeks is not the stated definition.
- E. This is the updated definition stated.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Persistent jaundice warrants evaluation, including consideration of conjugated bilirubin and treatable causes.

questions.stem: A term infant remains jaundiced at 3 weeks with pale stools and dark urine. Which type of hyperbilirubinemia should be suspected?
questions.initialExplanation: Pale stools and dark urine are characteristic of obstructive or cholestatic jaundice and suggest conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which requires investigation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the likely pattern given the cholestatic features.
- B. Crigler–Najjar type II causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
- C. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

- D. Breastfeeding jaundice is unconjugated and usually associated with low intake and dehydration early in life.
- E. Physiological unconjugated jaundice does not cause pale stools and dark urine.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Always assess stool and urine color in prolonged jaundice; pale stool is a red flag for cholestasis.

questions.stem: Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn classically occurs when:

options.label: A
options.text: Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus

options.label: B
options.text: Rh-positive mother carries an Rh-negative infant

options.label: C
options.text: Both mother and fetus are Rh-positive

options.label: E
options.text: Both mother and fetus are Rh-negative

questions.correctAnswerText: Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus
questions.initialExplanation: Rh disease can occur when an Rh-negative mother is sensitized to Rh-positive fetal red cells and produces maternal anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the classic Rh incompatibility pattern.
- B. This reverses the usual maternal-fetal Rh incompatibility.
- C. If both are Rh-positive, the mother is not sensitized to a foreign Rh D antigen in this way.
- D. ABO compatibility is a different system and is not the defining Rh mechanism.

- E. If both are Rh-negative, the Rh antigen target is absent.
questions.highYieldPoints: - An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus is at risk if sensitized.

questions.stem: Which investigation is typically positive in Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn?
questions.initialExplanation: The direct Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test is typically positive because maternal antibodies are bound to neonatal red blood cells.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Tensilon testing was historically used in myasthenia gravis.

- B. This supports antibody-mediated hemolysis in the newborn.
- C. Sweat chloride tests for cystic fibrosis.
- D. Hydrogen breath testing assesses carbohydrate malabsorption.
- E. Mantoux testing assesses tuberculosis sensitization.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Direct Coombs positivity supports antibody-mediated hemolysis.

questions.stem: When should anti-D immunoglobulin be administered to an eligible Rh-negative mother after delivery of an Rh-positive infant?
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that anti-D should be given to an Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive infant within 72 hours after delivery to prevent sensitization.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Within 72 hours is the recommended timing given.
- B. Two weeks is too late for the prophylaxis window stated.
- C. Prophylaxis is based on maternal-fetal Rh status, not waiting for jaundice.

- D. Six hours is not the only permitted interval described.
- E. Twenty-four hours is not the stated window.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Anti-D prophylaxis prevents maternal sensitization and is time-sensitive.

questions.stem: Which statement about ABO incompatibility is correct compared with Rh hemolytic disease?

options.label: A
options.text: It is often more common but generally less severe than Rh disease

options.label: B
options.text: It is usually more severe and more likely to cause hydrops

options.label: C
options.text: It typically causes severe anemia and hepatosplenomegaly

options.label: D
options.text: The direct Coombs test is typically negative

questions.correctAnswerText: It is often more common but generally less severe than Rh disease
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include ABO incompatibility as more common but usually less severe than Rh disease; some group O mothers have IgG anti-A or anti-B antibodies that cross the placenta.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the comparison stated.
- B. ABO disease is generally less severe than Rh disease.
- C. Severe anemia and hepatosplenomegaly are less typical than in severe Rh disease.
- D. The direct Coombs test may be positive.

- E. ABO incompatibility depends on ABO groups, not Rh-negative maternal status.
questions.highYieldPoints: - ABO disease is often milder; the mother is commonly group O and the infant group A or B.

questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes Crigler–Najjar syndrome type I from type II?

options.label: B
options.text: Type II is typically acquired after sepsis

options.label: C
options.text: Type I has absent glucuronyl transferase and is severe; type II has partial deficiency and may respond to phenobarbital

options.label: D
options.text: Type I is mild and responds to phenobarbital; type II causes severe kernicterus

options.label: E
options.text: Both types are caused by excess bilirubin production from hemolysis

questions.correctAnswerText: Type I has absent glucuronyl transferase and is severe; type II has partial deficiency and may respond to phenobarbital
questions.initialExplanation: Crigler–Najjar type I involves absent glucuronyl transferase and severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with risk of kernicterus; type II is partial deficiency and may respond to phenobarbital.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Both are unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia disorders.
- B. Type II is an inherited disorder, not an acquired post-sepsis condition.

- C. This is the comparison.
- D. This reverses the severity and response patterns.
- E. The primary defect is impaired conjugation, not excessive heme breakdown.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Type I: absent enzyme, severe; type II: partial deficiency, phenobarbital responsive.

questions.stem: A newborn develops jaundice during the first week, has poor milk intake, and shows signs of dehydration. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this pattern?
questions.initialExplanation: Breastfeeding jaundice occurs early and is associated with insufficient milk intake, reduced caloric intake, dehydration, and increased enterohepatic circulation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Physiological jaundice is predominantly unconjugated, not conjugated.

- B. This is the early low-intake pattern described for breastfeeding jaundice.
- C. Crigler–Najjar type I causes severe inherited impairment of bilirubin conjugation.
- D. Biliary atresia causes conjugated jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools.
- E. Breast milk jaundice usually appears from the second week in an otherwise well-hydrated infant.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Breastfeeding jaundice is related to inadequate intake and dehydration in the early days.

questions.stem: A thriving, well-hydrated, exclusively breastfed term infant develops persistent unconjugated jaundice from the second week. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.initialExplanation: Breast milk jaundice is a benign unconjugated jaundice of a healthy, well-hydrated breastfed infant, usually beginning in the second week and sometimes persisting for weeks.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Breastfeeding jaundice is earlier and associated with low milk intake and dehydration.
- B. Biliary atresia causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and pale stools.
- C. Sepsis is a pathological illness with systemic features.

- D. Rh disease causes immune hemolysis and usually presents earlier with anemia and unconjugated jaundice.
- E. This is the classic pattern of breast milk jaundice.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Differentiate early low-intake breastfeeding jaundice from later breast milk jaundice in a thriving infant.

questions.stem: How does phototherapy reduce unconjugated bilirubin?

options.label: A
options.text: It converts direct bilirubin into unconjugated bilirubin

options.label: C
options.text: It converts bilirubin into more water-soluble photoisomers that can be excreted

questions.correctAnswerText: It converts bilirubin into more water-soluble photoisomers that can be excreted
questions.initialExplanation: Blue-green light changes unconjugated bilirubin through photoisomerization and photo-oxidation into more water-soluble products that can be excreted in bile and urine.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Phototherapy acts on unconjugated bilirubin rather than converting direct bilirubin to indirect.

- B. Albumin synthesis is not its mechanism.
- C. This is the mechanism of phototherapy described.
- D. It does not intentionally increase enterohepatic circulation.
- E. Phototherapy does not treat jaundice by destroying red cells.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Phototherapy changes bilirubin into more water-soluble forms without requiring hepatic conjugation.

questions.stem: Why is phototherapy contraindicated in direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia?
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance warns against phototherapy in direct hyperbilirubinemia because it may cause bronze baby syndrome.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Surfactant deficiency causes RDS.
- B. Kernicterus is associated with free unconjugated bilirubin.
- C. Ductal closure is unrelated to phototherapy.

- D. Bronze baby syndrome is the complication specifically noted.
- E. Rh sensitization is an immune process unrelated to phototherapy.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Evaluate the bilirubin fraction before selecting phototherapy.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of exchange transfusion in severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?

options.label: A
options.text: Treat cholestasis by opening the bile ducts

options.label: C
options.text: Remove bilirubin and circulating antibodies while correcting anemia

options.label: E
options.text: Increase albumin binding without changing bilirubin

questions.correctAnswerText: Remove bilirubin and circulating antibodies while correcting anemia
questions.initialExplanation: Exchange transfusion removes toxic unconjugated bilirubin and maternal antibodies and can correct anemia in severe hemolytic disease.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. It does not correct biliary obstruction.
- B. It does not prevent neonatal infection.
- C. These are the main purposes described.
- D. It has no role in surfactant production.

- E. Exchange transfusion removes bilirubin rather than simply increasing albumin binding.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Exchange transfusion is reserved for bilirubin reaching dangerous levels or the relevant exchange threshold.

questions.stem: Which additional treatment may reduce the need for exchange transfusion in Rh or ABO hemolytic disease when bilirubin continues to rise despite intensive phototherapy?
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical guidance notes that IVIG may be used in Rh or ABO incompatibility when bilirubin continues to rise despite intensive phototherapy, reducing the need for exchange transfusion.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Caffeine is used for apnea of prematurity.
- B. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
- C. Iron is used to prevent or treat iron deficiency, not immune hemolysis.

- D. IVIG is the adjunctive treatment described for immune-mediated hemolysis.
- E. Pyridoxine is vitamin B6 and may be used in selected neonatal seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints: - IVIG may be considered in immune hemolysis when bilirubin rises despite intensive phototherapy.

questions.stem: Which parameter is used to determine whether a newborn needs no treatment, phototherapy, or exchange transfusion?

options.label: C
options.text: Total serum bilirubin plotted against age in hours

questions.correctAnswerText: Total serum bilirubin plotted against age in hours
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is plotting total serum bilirubin against the infant's age in hours to determine the treatment threshold.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Maternal hemoglobin does not determine neonatal bilirubin treatment.

- B. Apgar assesses newborn condition, not jaundice treatment thresholds.
- C. This is the decision method described for bilirubin treatment.
- D. Urine bilirubin alone does not determine treatment thresholds.
- E. Birth weight may affect risk but does not replace bilirubin plotting by age in hours.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Interpret bilirubin using age in hours and risk factors, not a single universal cutoff.

questions.stem: Kernicterus results from deposition of which substance in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei?
questions.initialExplanation: Kernicterus is bilirubin encephalopathy caused by deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Bile acids cause cholestatic effects, not bilirubin encephalopathy.
- B. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and can enter the brain when free bilirubin exceeds albumin-binding capacity.
- C. Iron deposition causes different neurological disorders.
- D. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and is not the cause of kernicterus.
- E. Calcium deposition is not the mechanism of kernicterus.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Free unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood–brain barrier and damage vulnerable nuclei.

questions.stem: Which factor increases the risk of bilirubin neurotoxicity in a preterm newborn?
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include prematurity, acidosis, sepsis, hypoxia, asphyxia, hypothermia, hypoalbuminemia, and some drugs as factors increasing bilirubin neurotoxicity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Normal albumin reduces the free unconjugated fraction.
- B. Absence of hypoxia is not a risk factor.
- C. Normothermia is protective compared with hypothermia.
- D. A mature blood–brain barrier is less vulnerable than the immature neonatal barrier.

- E. Acidosis and sepsis increase risk by affecting bilirubin binding and blood–brain barrier vulnerability.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Risk depends not only on total bilirubin but also albumin binding, prematurity, sepsis, acidosis, and hypoxia.

questions.stem: Which finding is an early manifestation of acute bilirubin encephalopathy?

options.label: A
options.text: Persistent opisthotonus and coma from the first symptom

options.label: D
options.text: Hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, and a high-pitched cry

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, and a high-pitched cry
questions.initialExplanation: Early acute bilirubin encephalopathy may present with hypotonia, lethargy, poor feeding, a high-pitched cry, and loss of the Moro reflex.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Opisthotonus, marked hypertonia, seizures, and coma are later manifestations.
- B. Ortolani testing assesses developmental dysplasia of the hip.
- C. Pale stool suggests cholestasis, not acute bilirubin encephalopathy.

- D. This is the early neurological pattern described.
- E. Club foot is an orthopedic abnormality.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Early signs can be subtle: poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, and high-pitched cry.

questions.stem: Which clinical feature is associated with the later stage of acute bilirubin encephalopathy?
questions.initialExplanation: Later acute bilirubin encephalopathy may cause hypertonia, arching or opisthotonus, seizures, coma, and death.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Delayed meconium passage suggests intestinal obstruction or Hirschsprung disease.
- B. An umbilical hernia is unrelated.

- C. This is the severe later neurological presentation described.
- D. Normal feeding and tone are reassuring findings.
- E. Acrocyanosis is a transient peripheral color change and unrelated.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Progression from early hypotonia to later hypertonia and opisthotonus is a classic pattern.

questions.stem: Which long-term neurological outcome may occur in survivors of chronic bilirubin encephalopathy?

options.label: B
options.text: Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy with sensorineural deafness

questions.correctAnswerText: Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy with sensorineural deafness
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy may result in choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, learning difficulties, sensorineural hearing loss, intellectual impairment, and seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Erb palsy is a birth-related brachial plexus injury.
- B. These are recognized long-term consequences of kernicterus.
- C. SMA is an anterior horn cell disorder.
- D. Ataxia-telangiectasia is an inherited DNA repair disorder.

- E. DMD is an inherited dystrophin disorder.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Kernicterus can cause dyskinetic CP and hearing impairment.

## Conjugated Hyperbilirubinemia and Biliary Atresia

questions.stem: Which finding meets standard definition of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?

options.label: B
options.text: Total bilirubin above 5 mg/dL at across the age range

options.label: D
options.text: Direct bilirubin above 2 mg/dL or more than 15% of total bilirubin

options.label: E
options.text: A bilirubin level that normalizes after feeding

questions.correctAnswerText: Direct bilirubin above 2 mg/dL or more than 15% of total bilirubin
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe conjugated hyperbilirubinemia as direct bilirubin greater than 2 mg/dL or more than 15% of total bilirubin.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Indirect bilirubin does not define conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
- B. Total bilirubin alone does not identify the bilirubin fraction.
- C. Urine bilirubin may be present because conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble.
- D. This is the threshold stated.
- E. Normalization after feeding is not the definition.
questions.highYieldPoints: - A raised direct fraction is pathological and requires evaluation for hepatobiliary disease.

questions.stem: Biliary atresia is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: Increased red-cell destruction from Rh antibodies

options.label: C
options.text: A transient deficiency of glucuronyl transferase

options.label: D
options.text: A developmental defect of the hip joint

options.label: E
options.text: Progressive fibrosis and obliteration of the biliary tree causing obstruction to bile flow

questions.correctAnswerText: Progressive fibrosis and obliteration of the biliary tree causing obstruction to bile flow
questions.initialExplanation: Biliary atresia is progressive fibrosis and obliteration of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic biliary tree, leading to cholestasis and progressive liver disease if untreated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Rh hemolysis causes unconjugated bilirubin overproduction.
- B. Surfactant deficiency causes neonatal RDS.
- C. Glucuronyl transferase deficiency causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
- D. Hip dysplasia is an orthopedic condition.

- E. This is the definition given.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Biliary atresia causes obstructive conjugated jaundice and requires early surgical management.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old infant has persistent jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and hepatomegaly. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
questions.initialExplanation: Biliary atresia presents with neonatal cholestasis, pale stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly; early diagnosis is essential.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Crigler–Najjar type II causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from impaired conjugation.

- B. Breast milk jaundice is unconjugated and occurs in a thriving breastfed infant with normally pigmented stools.
- C. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
- D. This is the classic clinical presentation of biliary atresia.
- E. Physiological jaundice is unconjugated and should not cause pale stools or dark urine.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Pale stools and dark urine in prolonged jaundice require urgent assessment for biliary atresia.

questions.stem: Which investigation may show good hepatic uptake but failure of tracer excretion into the intestine in biliary atresia?
questions.initialExplanation: Hepatobiliary scintigraphy may show tracer uptake by the liver but failure of excretion into the intestine in biliary atresia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hip ultrasound screens for DDH.

- B. EEG assesses cerebral electrical activity.
- C. Nerve conduction studies evaluate peripheral nerves.
- D. Cranial ultrasound evaluates brain structures.
- E. This describes the HIDA scan pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints: - HIDA: uptake without bowel excretion supports impaired bile flow, though further evaluation is required.

questions.stem: What is the preferred surgical procedure for biliary atresia, with the best chance of success when performed early?
questions.initialExplanation: The Kasai operation (hepatoportoenterostomy) is the primary surgical treatment for biliary atresia; An important point is improved success when performed before 60 days of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. VP shunt treats hydrocephalus.
- B. Pyloromyotomy treats hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
- C. This is the operation used to restore bile drainage in biliary atresia.
- D. Fundoplication treats selected severe gastroesophageal reflux.
- E. Pavlik harness treats developmental dysplasia of the hip.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Early Kasai surgery improves outcome; liver transplantation may be needed if it fails.

## Hypoxic Ischemic Encephalopathy

questions.stem: Perinatal asphyxia is defined as impaired gas exchange leading to which physiological changes?
questions.initialExplanation: Impaired gas exchange at the placenta or lungs causes progressive hypoxemia, hypercarbia, and acidosis in perinatal asphyxia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hypocalcemia may occur in HIE but is not the defining gas-exchange abnormality.
- B. This is the pathophysiological sequence described.
- C. Hyperglycemia alone does not define perinatal asphyxia.
- D. Gas exchange impairment reduces oxygen delivery rather than increasing it.

- E. This is the opposite physiological pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Perinatal asphyxia produces hypoxemia, carbon dioxide retention, and metabolic or mixed acidosis.

questions.stem: Which combination is included among the essential characteristics of perinatal asphyxia described?

options.label: B
options.text: Severe cord blood acidosis, low Apgar persisting beyond 5 minutes, neurological manifestations, and multiorgan dysfunction

options.label: C
options.text: A transient peripheral cyanosis with normal oxygenation

options.label: D
options.text: Jaundice after day 3 without other symptoms

options.label: E
options.text: A single low blood glucose measurement

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe cord blood acidosis, low Apgar persisting beyond 5 minutes, neurological manifestations, and multiorgan dysfunction
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include profound metabolic or mixed acidosis, a very low Apgar score persisting beyond 5 minutes, neurological manifestations, and multiorgan dysfunction as essential characteristics.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hip examination findings are unrelated.
- B. This combines the four essential features listed.
- C. Peripheral cyanosis with normal oxygenation does not establish perinatal asphyxia.

- D. Physiological jaundice is common and does not define asphyxia.
- E. Hypoglycemia alone is insufficient to define perinatal asphyxia.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Perinatal asphyxia is a multisystem clinical diagnosis, not a single low Apgar score alone.

questions.stem: A newborn with mild HIE is typically described as:

options.label: A
options.text: Having severe fixed opisthotonus from birth

options.label: B
options.text: Stuporous and comatose with flaccid tone

options.label: C
options.text: Hyperalert and irritable with increased responses to stimulation

options.label: D
options.text: Flaccid with absent reflexes and refractory seizures

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperalert and irritable with increased responses to stimulation
questions.initialExplanation: Mild HIE (stage 1) may present with irritability, hyperalertness, excessive response to stimulation, staring, or hyperventilation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Fixed severe posturing is not the typical mild-stage presentation.

- B. Stupor, coma, and flaccidity indicate severe HIE.
- C. This is the mild HIE pattern described.
- D. Flaccidity and refractory seizures indicate severe disease.
- E. Unresponsiveness with multiorgan failure is severe HIE.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Stage 1: hyperalert/irritable; Stage 2: lethargic/hypotonic; Stage 3: stupor/coma/flaccid.

questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with moderate (stage 2) HIE?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal neurological examination with no feeding difficulty

options.label: B
options.text: Lethargy, hypotonia, weak Moro reflex, and seizures may occur

options.label: C
options.text: Stupor, coma, flaccidity, and absent reflexes in typical presentations

options.label: D
options.text: Hyperalert state with normal tone and no seizures

questions.correctAnswerText: Lethargy, hypotonia, weak Moro reflex, and seizures may occur
questions.initialExplanation: Moderate HIE is characterized by lethargy, hypotonia, abnormal movements, weak Moro reflex, feeding difficulty, and possible seizures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Moderate HIE often causes neurological and feeding abnormalities.
- B. This matches the moderate stage described.
- C. This is the severe stage.
- D. This is closer to mild HIE.
- E. Isolated jaundice does not define moderate HIE.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Moderate HIE often produces lethargy, hypotonia, poor feeding, and seizures.

questions.stem: Which EEG pattern is associated with severe HIE 's staging table?

options.label: A
options.text: Burst suppression progressing toward an isoelectric pattern

questions.correctAnswerText: Burst suppression progressing toward an isoelectric pattern
questions.initialExplanation: Severe HIE may produce burst suppression progressing toward an isoelectric EEG pattern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the severe EEG pattern.
- B. A normal EEG is more consistent with mild HIE.
- C. Three-Hz spike-and-wave is associated with typical absence epilepsy.
- D. Low voltage may occur in moderate HIE but is not the severe pattern described.
- E. Hypsarrhythmia is associated with infantile spasms.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Severe HIE is associated with profound suppression of cerebral electrical activity.

questions.stem: Which therapeutic intervention may reduce mortality and brain injury in selected term or near-term infants with moderate or severe HIE?
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include therapeutic hypothermia, initiated within the first 6 hours and maintained at a target temperature around 33–34°C for 72 hours in eligible infants, as reducing mortality and morbidity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Exchange transfusion is not routine HIE treatment.
- B. Overheating may worsen brain injury.
- C. High-dose oral feeding does not provide neuroprotection and may be unsafe in encephalopathic infants.

- D. Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, not HIE.
- E. Therapeutic hypothermia is the neuroprotective intervention described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Cooling is time-critical and eligibility should follow current neonatal protocols.

## Neonatal Seizures

questions.stem: Neonatal polycythemia is defined by a central venous hematocrit greater than:
questions.initialExplanation: Standard definitions describe neonatal polycythemia as a central venous hematocrit or packed cell volume above 65%.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Forty-five percent is not the threshold stated.
- B. Sixty percent is below the threshold.
- C. Above 65% is the stated definition of neonatal polycythemia.

- D. Fifty-five percent is below the definition.
- E. Fifty percent is below the definition.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Use a central venous hematocrit >65% as the threshold in this standard guidance.

questions.stem: Which condition can cause neonatal polycythemia through chronic intrauterine hypoxia and increased erythropoietin production?
questions.initialExplanation: Chronic intrauterine hypoxia, including that associated with IUGR, maternal diabetes, or smoking, can stimulate fetal erythropoietin and increase red-cell mass.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. TTN results from delayed lung-fluid clearance.
- B. Congenital hypothyroidism is not the mechanism described.
- C. Choanal atresia causes upper airway obstruction.

- D. IUGR and chronic fetal hypoxia are recognized causes of neonatal polycythemia.
- E. Breast milk jaundice is an unconjugated bilirubin condition.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Chronic fetal hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin and increases neonatal hematocrit.

questions.stem: Which management is used for symptomatic neonatal polycythemia with hyperviscosity?
questions.initialExplanation: Partial exchange transfusion reduces hematocrit and blood viscosity in selected symptomatic infants with neonatal polycythemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Kasai surgery treats biliary atresia.
- B. Phototherapy treats unconjugated jaundice and does not reduce hematocrit.
- C. Iron is not the acute treatment for hyperviscosity.

- D. This is the treatment described for significant symptomatic polycythemia.
- E. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Assess symptoms and venous hematocrit; partial exchange is considered in selected symptomatic or markedly elevated cases.

questions.stem: What is the expected hemoglobin pattern in physiological anemia of a term newborn?

options.label: A
options.text: Hemoglobin falls if there is hemolysis

options.label: B
options.text: Hemoglobin rises continuously during the first 12 weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Hemoglobin remains at the birth level throughout infancy

options.label: D
options.text: Hemoglobin falls to zero by 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.text: Hemoglobin falls to approximately 10–11 g/dL around 8–12 weeks

questions.correctAnswerText: Hemoglobin falls to approximately 10–11 g/dL around 8–12 weeks
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include a physiological fall in hemoglobin from the higher neonatal level to approximately 10–11 g/dL at 8–12 weeks of age.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. The physiological fall occurs even without hemolysis.

- B. Hemoglobin normally declines during early infancy rather than rising continuously.
- C. Hemoglobin does not remain at the birth level throughout infancy.
- D. A fall to zero is incompatible with life and not physiological.
- E. This is the physiological nadir described.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Physiological anemia of infancy is a normal postnatal decline in hemoglobin.

questions.stem: Which statement about physiological anemia in a healthy term infant is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: It is caused by vitamin K deficiency

options.label: C
options.text: It is diagnosed by prolonged PT and PTT

options.label: E
options.text: It is typically associated with severe hemolysis

questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that physiological anemia in term infants does not require treatment; preterm infants may need iron supplementation because of lower stores and rapid growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. This is the management described for term infants.
- B. Vitamin K deficiency causes hemorrhagic disease, not physiological anemia.
- C. Prolonged PT and PTT are associated with vitamin K deficiency coagulopathy.
- D. Transfusion is not required for physiological anemia in a healthy term infant.
- E. Severe hemolysis is not the mechanism of physiological anemia.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Physiological anemia is expected in term infants; preterm infants have additional iron needs.

questions.stem: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns affects which coagulation factors?

options.label: C
options.text: Factors II, VII, IX, and X

options.label: D
options.text: Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII

questions.correctAnswerText: Factors II, VII, IX, and X
questions.initialExplanation: Vitamin K is required for synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X; deficiency may cause neonatal bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Factors XI and XII are not the factors described.
- B. Vitamin K deficiency affects coagulation factor synthesis rather than platelet count itself.

- C. This is the correct group of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors.
- D. These are not the vitamin K-dependent factors listed.
- E. Factors V and VIII are not vitamin K-dependent.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, and X.

questions.stem: Which factor contributes to vitamin K deficiency bleeding in exclusively breastfed newborns?

options.label: A
options.text: Vitamin K is water-soluble and cannot be absorbed

options.label: B
options.text: Breast milk has relatively low vitamin K content

options.label: C
options.text: Newborns have fully mature hepatic synthesis of clotting factors

options.label: D
options.text: Newborns have a mature intestinal flora at birth

options.label: E
options.text: Breast milk contains excessive vitamin K

questions.correctAnswerText: Breast milk has relatively low vitamin K content
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include low vitamin K stores, low vitamin K intake from breast milk, absent intestinal flora at birth, and immature liver function as predisposing factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Vitamin K is fat-soluble, not water-soluble.

- B. Low vitamin K content of breast milk contributes to risk.
- C. Hepatic synthetic capacity is immature in newborns, especially preterm infants.
- D. The newborn gut is initially sterile and has little bacterial vitamin K synthesis.
- E. Breast milk is relatively low in vitamin K rather than excessive.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Newborns have low stores, low dietary intake, limited gut synthesis, and immature liver function.

questions.stem: Classical vitamin K deficiency bleeding most commonly presents during which period?
questions.initialExplanation: Classical vitamin K deficiency bleeding typically presents between the second and seventh day of life, often when prophylaxis has not been given.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Days 2–7 are the classical presentation period stated.
- B. Six to twelve months is not the neonatal classical period.
- C. Adolescence is unrelated.

- D. Bleeding within the first 24 hours is very rare and may reflect maternal drug effects or other causes.
- E. After one year is outside the neonatal period.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Classical vitamin K deficiency bleeding occurs in the first week, usually days 2–7.

questions.stem: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding is more strongly associated with which clinical complication?
questions.initialExplanation: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, typically at 2–8 weeks, is associated with liver disease or malabsorption and has a higher frequency of intracranial hemorrhage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pyloric stenosis is a gastric outlet obstruction.
- B. PDA is a cardiovascular complication of prematurity.
- C. Cleft palate is a congenital orofacial anomaly.
- D. Intracranial hemorrhage is particularly important in late vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
- E. Physiological weight loss is an expected early neonatal change.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding is dangerous because intracranial hemorrhage is more common.

questions.stem: Which coagulation profile is expected in vitamin K deficiency bleeding?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal coagulation studies in each case

options.label: B
options.text: Short PT and prolonged bleeding time

options.label: C
options.text: Prolonged PT and PTT with normal platelet count

options.label: D
options.text: Positive direct Coombs test with low hemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: Normal PT and PTT with severe thrombocytopenia

questions.correctAnswerText: Prolonged PT and PTT with normal platelet count
questions.initialExplanation: Clinical descriptions include prolonged PT and PTT with a normal platelet count in vitamin K deficiency bleeding; bleeding time is usually normal.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Coagulation studies are abnormal in vitamin K deficiency.

- B. The pattern described is prolonged clotting times rather than shortened PT.
- C. This is the typical coagulation profile described.
- D. Direct Coombs testing evaluates antibody-mediated hemolysis.
- E. Severe thrombocytopenia is not the defining abnormality.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Vitamin K deficiency affects clotting-factor activity, not platelet number.

questions.stem: Which statement about prevention of vitamin K deficiency bleeding is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Vitamin K is given if bleeding occurs

options.label: B
options.text: Breastfed infants should avoid vitamin K

options.label: C
options.text: Vitamin K is given at 6 months

options.label: D
options.text: newborns should receive vitamin K at birth

options.label: E
options.text: preterm infants require vitamin K prophylaxis

questions.correctAnswerText: newborns should receive vitamin K at birth
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that all newborns should receive vitamin K prophylaxis at birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Waiting for bleeding is unsafe because hemorrhage may be severe.
- B. Breastfed infants are at particular risk because breast milk is relatively low in vitamin K.
- C. Six months is not the timing for neonatal prophylaxis.

- D. Universal newborn vitamin K prophylaxis is recommended.
- E. Term infants also require prophylaxis.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Vitamin K prophylaxis is a routine preventive measure for all newborns.

## Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

questions.stem: Which newborn has the greatest risk profile for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)?

options.label: B
options.text: A term infant with transient acrocyanosis

options.label: C
options.text: A first-born girl with breech presentation and a positive family history

options.label: D
options.text: A second-born boy in cephalic presentation with no family history

options.label: E
options.text: A preterm infant with physiological jaundice

questions.correctAnswerText: A first-born girl with breech presentation and a positive family history
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include female sex, first-born status, breech presentation, positive family history, and left-sided involvement as important DDH risk factors.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Neonatal acne is unrelated.

- B. Acrocyanosis is unrelated to hip development.
- C. This infant has several major DDH risk factors.
- D. This infant lacks the risk factors highlighted.
- E. Prematurity and physiological jaundice alone are not the principal DDH risk factors listed.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Remember the DDH risk-factor cluster: female, first-born, breech, family history.

questions.stem: Which maneuver is used to detect a dislocatable hip in a newborn?
questions.initialExplanation: The Barlow maneuver attempts to dislocate an unstable hip, whereas the Ortolani maneuver attempts to relocate a dislocated hip.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Babinski is a plantar response.

- B. Ortolani is used to reduce a dislocated hip.
- C. Moro is a primitive reflex.
- D. Galeazzi compares knee heights when hips and knees are flexed.
- E. Barlow tests whether the hip is dislocatable.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Barlow = dislocatable hip; Ortolani = relocation of a dislocated hip.

questions.stem: Which maneuver is used to relocate a dislocated femoral head into the acetabulum?
questions.initialExplanation: The Ortolani maneuver abducts the flexed hip and relocates a dislocated femoral head into the acetabulum.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Ortolani attempts reduction of a dislocated hip.
- B. Barlow attempts to dislocate an unstable hip.
- C. Galeazzi identifies limb-length discrepancy by comparing knee heights.
- D. Square window test is part of the Ballard score.

- E. Scarf sign is part of neuromuscular maturity assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Ortolani = relocation; Barlow = provocation of dislocation.

questions.stem: A newborn has one knee lower than the other when both hips and knees are flexed. Which sign is positive?
questions.initialExplanation: A positive Galeazzi sign is a difference in knee height when both hips and knees are flexed, suggesting hip dislocation or limb-length discrepancy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Kernig is a meningeal irritation sign.
- B. Gower demonstrates proximal muscle weakness.
- C. This is the sign described for DDH.
- D. Rovsing is an appendicitis sign.

- E. Brudzinski is another meningeal irritation sign.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Galeazzi compares knee heights with hips and knees flexed.

questions.stem: Which imaging modality is preferred for early evaluation of developmental dysplasia of the hip in a young infant?

options.label: B
options.text: AP pelvic X-ray in the first week

questions.initialExplanation: Hip ultrasound is used for early assessment and screening of high-risk newborns; pelvic radiography becomes more useful after approximately 4–6 months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Spinal MRI does not assess hip joint development.
- B. Pelvic X-ray is less useful before sufficient ossification and is used later.
- C. CT is not the routine first-line screening study.
- D. Abdominal ultrasound is not a hip study.

- E. Ultrasound is the early imaging modality described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ultrasound early; AP pelvis X-ray after about 4–6 months.

## Congenital Talipes Equinovarus

questions.stem: Which conservative device is commonly used in early treatment of DDH?
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include the Pavlik harness as a treatment for DDH, with hip spica or surgery considered in selected cases or when conservative treatment fails.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. A knee immobilizer does not treat hip dysplasia.
- B. Pavlik harness is the conservative treatment listed.
- C. A cervical collar treats neck conditions.
- D. An ankle-foot orthosis treats selected foot or ankle problems.

- E. Hip spica may be used in selected cases, but is not the only treatment in every newborn.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Pavlik harness is commonly used in early DDH management.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes true congenital talipes equinovarus from positional talipes?

options.label: A
options.text: Positional talipes requires immediate open surgery

options.label: B
options.text: True clubfoot is typically painless and requires no treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Positional talipes is typically fixed and bilateral

options.label: D
options.text: True clubfoot is typically caused by delivery trauma

options.label: E
options.text: True clubfoot is fixed and cannot be fully corrected by passive manipulation

questions.correctAnswerText: True clubfoot is fixed and cannot be fully corrected by passive manipulation
questions.initialExplanation: True talipes equinovarus is fixed and cannot be completely corrected by passive manipulation; positional talipes is usually due to intrauterine compression and can be corrected toward neutral.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Positional talipes often improves with passive manipulation and does not require immediate open surgery.
- B. True clubfoot requires orthopedic treatment.

- C. Positional talipes is generally flexible and correctable.
- D. True clubfoot may be idiopathic, familial, or secondary to conditions such as oligohydramnios or neuromuscular disorders.
- E. This is the key distinction described.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Fixed deformity suggests true clubfoot; flexible correctable deformity suggests positional talipes.

## Maturity Assessment (Ballard Score)

questions.stem: Which treatment method is listed for congenital talipes equinovarus?
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include orthopedic management with plaster casting and bracing using the Ponseti method; surgery may be required in selected cases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis.

- B. Ponseti casting and bracing are standard orthopedic measures described.
- C. Exchange transfusion treats selected severe hemolytic jaundice.
- D. Phototherapy treats neonatal jaundice.
- E. Kasai treats biliary atresia.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Ponseti serial casting followed by bracing is a key treatment approach for clubfoot.

questions.stem: Which set of physical findings is assessed in the physical maturity component of the New Ballard score?

options.label: C
options.text: Skin, lanugo, ear cartilage/recoil, breast tissue, genitalia, and sole creases

options.label: D
options.text: Apgar score, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation

questions.correctAnswerText: Skin, lanugo, ear cartilage/recoil, breast tissue, genitalia, and sole creases
questions.initialExplanation: The physical maturity section of the Ballard score assesses skin, lanugo, ear cartilage and recoil, eye findings, breast size, genitalia, and plantar creases.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Imaging is not part of the physical maturity score.

- B. Laboratory values are not components of Ballard scoring.
- C. These are the physical findings used in the score.
- D. Apgar and vital signs assess immediate condition, not gestational maturity.
- E. Primitive reflexes are assessed clinically but are not the physical maturity components listed.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Ballard physical maturity includes skin, hair, ear, breast, genital, and sole findings.
