## Primitive Reflexes

questions.stem: Which group of findings belongs to the neuromuscular component of the New Ballard score?

options.label: B
options.text: Posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle, and heel-to-ear

options.label: E
options.text: Skin color, breast size, and genital maturity

questions.correctAnswerText: Posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle, and heel-to-ear
questions.initialExplanation: The neuromuscular component of the New Ballard score includes posture, square window, arm recoil, scarf sign, popliteal angle, and heel-to-ear maneuver.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Electrolytes and glucose are laboratory values, not Ballard components.

- B. These are the neuromuscular signs listed in the Ballard score.
- C. Apgar appearance and pulse assess immediate adaptation.
- D. Primitive reflexes are neurological examination findings, not the six neuromuscular Ballard maneuvers.
- E. These are physical maturity findings.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Know the six neuromuscular Ballard maneuvers.

questions.stem: Primitive neonatal reflexes are mediated mainly at which level?

options.label: D
options.text: Subcortical level because the cerebral cortex is functionally immature

questions.correctAnswerText: Subcortical level because the cerebral cortex is functionally immature
questions.initialExplanation: Primitive reflexes are mediated at the subcortical level because the cerebral cortex is still functionally immature; they gradually disappear as cortical control matures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. The cerebral cortex is not the sole mediator of primitive reflexes.
- B. The cerebellum is not the primary level described.
- C. Autonomic ganglia do not mediate the full range of primitive neonatal reflexes.
- D. This is the explanation given.
- E. Primitive reflexes involve central subcortical pathways, not only peripheral nerves.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Primitive reflexes reflect early subcortical control and are integrated as the cortex matures.

questions.stem: What is the significance of an asymmetrical primitive reflex response in a newborn?

options.label: B
options.text: It may indicate a focal neurological deficit

questions.correctAnswerText: It may indicate a focal neurological deficit
questions.initialExplanation: It is recognized that normal neonatal reflexes indicate normal neurological status, while an asymmetrical response may indicate a focal neurological deficit.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Hypoglycemia may cause neurological signs but is not diagnosed by asymmetry alone.
- B. Asymmetry can indicate a focal neurological lesion or peripheral injury.
- C. Sepsis is not diagnosed by primitive reflex asymmetry alone.
- D. The finding is clinically important and warrants assessment.

- E. A symmetrical response is generally reassuring; asymmetry is not normal by definition.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Asymmetry is a warning sign and should prompt a focused neurological and musculoskeletal examination.

questions.stem: When the cheek of a newborn is stroked, the infant turns the head toward the stimulus and opens the mouth. Which reflex is elicited?
questions.initialExplanation: The rooting reflex is elicited by stroking the cheek; the infant turns toward the stimulus and opens the mouth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Palmar grasp occurs when the palm is stimulated.
- B. This is the description of the rooting reflex.
- C. Parachute is a protective extension response that appears later.

- D. Moro involves extension and abduction of the arms followed by flexion and adduction.
- E. Stepping involves alternate leg movements when held upright with feet touching a surface.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Rooting helps the newborn locate the breast or bottle.

questions.stem: Which maneuver elicits the Moro reflex?

options.label: A
options.text: Turning the head to one side while lying supine

options.label: B
options.text: Touching the sole at the base of the toes

options.label: C
options.text: Touching the palm with the examiner's thumb

options.label: D
options.text: A sudden change in support or gentle drop of the head while supported

questions.correctAnswerText: A sudden change in support or gentle drop of the head while supported
questions.initialExplanation: The Moro reflex is elicited by a sudden change in support or gentle movement of the supported infant; the arms extend and abduct with opening of the hands, then flex and adduct.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Turning the head elicits the asymmetric tonic neck reflex.

- B. Touching the sole elicits plantar grasp.
- C. Touching the palm elicits palmar grasp.
- D. This is the stimulus and response described for Moro.
- E. Stroking the cheek elicits rooting.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Moro: extension/abduction and opening of hands, followed by flexion/adduction.

questions.stem: Which statement about the parachute reflex is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a sign of congenital hip dislocation

options.label: B
options.text: It appears after about 7 months and persists

options.label: C
options.text: It is the same as the palmar grasp reflex

options.label: D
options.text: It is elicited by stroking the cheek

options.label: E
options.text: It is present during the first week and disappears

questions.correctAnswerText: It appears after about 7 months and persists
questions.initialExplanation: The forward parachute reflex appears after approximately 7 months and persists as a protective response.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Parachute is a postural protective reflex, not a hip test.

- B. This is the timing and persistence described.
- C. Palmar grasp is a different primitive reflex.
- D. Stroking the cheek elicits rooting.
- E. The parachute response appears later, not in the first week.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Parachute is a later protective reaction and persists rather than integrating like early primitive reflexes.

questions.stem: A newborn is held upright with the soles of the feet touching a flat surface. The infant makes alternating stepping-like leg movements. Which reflex is being elicited?
questions.initialExplanation: The stepping reflex is elicited by holding the infant upright with the feet touching a surface, producing alternating flexion and extension of the legs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Moro involves arm extension and abduction followed by flexion and adduction.
- B. This is the stepping response described.
- C. Palmar grasp is elicited by stimulating the palm.

- D. Rooting is elicited by stroking the cheek.
- E. Placing is elicited by touching the dorsum of the foot against the edge of a surface.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Stepping: upright suspension with the feet touching the surface produces alternating leg movements.

questions.stem: The dorsum of a newborn's foot is brought against the edge of an examination table. The infant flexes the hip and knee and lifts the foot onto the surface. Which reflex is this?
questions.initialExplanation: The placing reflex is elicited by touching the dorsal surface of the foot against the edge of a table, causing flexion and lifting as if stepping onto it.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Parachute is a protective extension reaction that appears later.

- B. This is the placing response described.
- C. Moro is a startle response involving the arms.
- D. ATNR occurs with head turning and produces a fencing posture.
- E. Stepping involves alternate leg movements when the soles contact a surface.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Placing: touch the dorsum of the foot to an edge and observe the stepping-up response.

questions.stem: When a supine newborn's head is turned to one side, the arm and leg on that side extend while the opposite limbs flex. Which reflex is present?
questions.initialExplanation: The asymmetric tonic neck reflex is elicited by turning the infant's head to one side, producing extension of the limbs on the face side and flexion of the opposite limbs.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Moro is elicited by a sudden change in support.
- B. Galant is elicited by stroking the paraspinal region and causes trunk curvature.
- C. Plantar grasp causes toe flexion when the sole is stimulated.

- D. This is the classic fencing posture of the asymmetric tonic neck reflex.
- E. Rooting is elicited by cheek stimulation.
questions.highYieldPoints: - ATNR produces a fencing posture when the head is turned.

questions.stem: Touching the palm of a newborn produces finger flexion around the examiner's thumb. Which reflex is elicited?
questions.initialExplanation: The palmar grasp reflex is elicited by placing a finger or thumb against the palm, producing finger flexion and grasp.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Stepping is elicited by holding the infant upright with feet touching a surface.
- B. Rooting is elicited by stroking the cheek.
- C. Plantar grasp is elicited by stimulating the sole near the toes and causes toe flexion.
- D. Moro is a startle reflex.

- E. This is the palmar grasp response.
questions.highYieldPoints: - Palmar grasp: stimulate the palm and observe finger flexion.

questions.stem: Lightly stroking the skin alongside the newborn's spine causes the hips and buttocks to curve toward the stimulated side. Which reflex is this?
questions.initialExplanation: The Galant reflex is elicited by lightly stroking alongside the spine, causing lateral flexion of the trunk and hips toward the stimulus.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Sucking is elicited by stimulation of the lips or insertion of a finger into the mouth.
- B. Moro involves a startle response with arm extension and subsequent flexion.
- C. This is the Galant or truncal incurvation response.
- D. Parachute is a protective extension response that develops later.

- E. Placing is elicited by touching the dorsum of the foot to an edge.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Galant: paraspinal stimulation causes the trunk to curve toward the stimulus.


## Supplementary Exam Practice — Targeted Curriculum Gaps

topics.name: Supplementary Exam Practice — Targeted Curriculum Gaps

questions.stem: A baby is born at 35 completed weeks and weighs 1,400 g. Which paired classification is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Post-term and extremely low birth weight

options.label: B
options.text: Term and very low birth weight

options.label: E
options.text: Preterm and very low birth weight

questions.correctAnswerText: Preterm and very low birth weight
questions.initialExplanation: Birth before 37 completed weeks is preterm; a birth weight below 1,500 g is very low birth weight.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: The infant is neither post-term nor below 1,000 g.
- B. Incorrect: Both parts are incorrect for the stated gestation and weight.
- C. Incorrect: The infant is not term and is below 2,500 g.
- D. Incorrect: The baby is preterm, but 1,400 g is not normal birth weight.

- E. Correct: 35 weeks is preterm, and 1,400 g is VLBW.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- Preterm: before 37 completed weeks.
- LBW <2,500 g; VLBW <1,500 g; ELBW <1,000 g.

questions.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, a newborn remains apnoeic and the heart rate is 80/min after initial steps. What is the next priority?

options.label: D
options.text: Begin effective positive-pressure ventilation and assess chest movement/heart-rate response

questions.correctAnswerText: Begin effective positive-pressure ventilation and assess chest movement/heart-rate response
questions.initialExplanation: An apnoeic newborn with HR below 100/min requires effective ventilation; chest compressions are considered only if HR remains below 60/min despite adequate ventilation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: Compressions are indicated when HR remains below 60/min after adequate ventilation.
- B. Incorrect: Delay is unsafe in a compromised newborn.
- C. Incorrect: Oral glucose does not treat neonatal apnoea or bradycardia.

- D. Correct: Positive-pressure ventilation is the priority for apnoea or HR below 100/min.
- E. Incorrect: Bicarbonate is not the first response to neonatal bradycardia.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- In neonatal resuscitation, effective ventilation is the key initial intervention for apnoea/gasping or HR below 100/min.
- Reassess heart rate after ventilation; compressions follow if HR remains below 60/min despite effective ventilation.

questions.stem: A term infant delivered by elective Caesarean section develops early tachypnoea, but improves over the next 24–48 hours. Chest X-ray shows prominent perihilar markings and fluid in the fissures. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Respiratory distress syndrome due to surfactant deficiency

questions.initialExplanation: Early respiratory distress after Caesarean delivery with radiographic retained lung fluid and rapid improvement is typical of transient tachypnoea of the newborn.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Correct: TTN is caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid and usually resolves over 24–72 hours.
- B. Incorrect: Meconium aspiration is associated with meconium exposure and patchy hyperinflation/opacities.
- C. Incorrect: Pneumonia may have systemic/infective features and does not have this classic rapid self-limited pattern.

- D. Incorrect: RDS is associated with surfactant deficiency and typically has diffuse reticulogranular changes, especially in preterm infants.
- E. Incorrect: CDH usually causes severe respiratory distress with scaphoid abdomen and bowel in the chest.
questions.highYieldPoints:
- TTN: delayed fetal lung-fluid clearance; risk rises after Caesarean delivery.
- Differentiate TTN from RDS and MAS using gestation, risk factors, radiology and clinical course.

questions.stem: A healthy term newborn develops visible jaundice at 12 hours of life. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Physiological jaundice is expected in the first 12 hours

options.label: C
options.text: It is typically due to biliary atresia

options.label: E
options.text: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise

questions.correctAnswerText: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise
questions.initialExplanation: Jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours is an early warning sign and requires urgent assessment for pathological causes such as haemolysis or infection.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A. Incorrect: Physiological jaundice generally appears after the first 24 hours, not at 12 hours.
- B. Incorrect: Breast-milk jaundice occurs later and is not the explanation for jaundice at 12 hours.
- C. Incorrect: Biliary atresia causes conjugated jaundice, usually later and persistent, not every early neonatal jaundice.

- D. Incorrect: Bilirubin measurement and clinical assessment are needed.
- E. Correct: Jaundice in the first day is pathological until evaluated.
